title: Power Is More Relevant Than Ascensional Speed to Determine Metabolic Demand at Different Gradient Slopes During Running
authors: Hingrand C, Olivier N, Combes A, Bensaid S, Daussin FN
journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
population: 10 subjects (8 men, 2 women) performing incremental tests at 1%, 10% and 25% slope; ascensional speed increment 100 m/h every minute on the 10% and 25% tests
findings: VO2max was similar in the three conditions (68.7 +/- 6.2, 70.1 +/- 7.3 and 67.6 +/- 7.0 for 1%, 10% and 25%).
The maximal ascensional speed reached was greater at 25% than at 10% (1,760 +/- 190 vs 1,330 +/- 106 m/h, p < 0.01).
Relative VO2 related to relative power with no effect of slope.
The authors conclude that power, not ascensional speed, should prescribe training intensity in trail running.
limitations: 10 subjects (2 women), incremental ramp tests, three slopes; no field or race data; power estimation method is not described in the abstract.
implications: Do not use one vertical-speed (m/h) target as a fixed intensity across different gradients: the same effort yielded about 32% higher ascent speed at 25% than at 10% slope (1,760 vs 1,330 m/h, derived).
Prescribe climbing effort by power or effort-equivalent flat pace (a grade-adjusted measure) rather than by vertical speed alone.

verification.notes: Added. Crossref: J Strength Cond Res 37(11):2298-2301, 2023, five authors match (Crossref title has HTML entity for ampersand in journal name only). PubMed PMID 37883404 abstract supports all numbers; the 32% figure is derived.
